st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s task- and dimension-specific account of benchmark success by benchmarking citation verification itself. It shows that strong detection of basic defects does not translate into dependable checking of pinpoint citations, quotations or substantive source support, while longitudinal results indicate that citation hallucinations have not consistently declined.

Taken together, we make the following contributions:    • We provide longitudinal empirical evidence, across eight ChatGPT models from late 2023 through       late 2025, that legal citation hallucination rates do not consistently decline, while the number of       hallucinated court filings grows steadily.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The source accepts that AI-enabled participation alone does not secure effective access to justice and materially develops the cluster’s verification agenda. It proposes court-provided AI literacy, citation-checking support and free legal-data infrastructure to make responsible use more feasible for self-represented litigants, while offering recommendations rather than evidence of improved remedies.
qs: First, we need effective interventions that educate pro se litigants on how to use AI tools responsi- bly and equip them with best practices and tools for verifying AI-generated citations.
Second, expanding public, freely-available access to legal data (including all case law) would improve both human and automated citation veri- fication performance for under-resourced filers.

kp.k: Citation hallucination rates do not consistently decline
kp.d: Liu, Stammbach and Henderson report a controlled experiment across eight ChatGPT generations from late 2023 through late 2025, using the same 92 legal-drafting prompts and producing over 8,000 case citations checked against CourtListener and Westlaw. Early GPT-3.5 models hallucinated around 25% of citations; mid-2024 GPT-4o models reached 1.23%, whereas GPT-5.1 reached 6.57%, significantly above the August 2024 GPT-4o release (p = 0.001). Their definition covers nonexistent cases and case-name/reporter mismatches, excluding unsupported propositions attributed to real cases, so these results are a conservative measure rather than an overall legal-error rate.
qs: The prompts ask the LLM to generate documents similar to the ones flagged in real court filings because of AI-generated hallu- cinations (examples in Appendix Table A3), producing over 8,000 case citations in total.
Subtler misrepresentations, such as citing a real case for a non-supported proposition, are not captured by this criterion.

kp.k: Cheaper drafting can increase human checking burdens
kp.d: The authors identify over 1,000 filings containing hallucinated citations through their research and public datasets, reporting steady growth despite sanctions. Separately, their drafting experiment finds that newer models generate more citations and cite less canonical cases: GPT-3.5-generated cases had median citation counts above 500, versus a low of 105 for GPT-4o. They argue that these changes make checking harder and shift unchecked work onto opposing counsel, law clerks and judges. Their Jevons-paradox argument—that cheaper drafting will increase total filing volume—is a prediction, distinct from the observed citation-generation results.
qs: Newer models produce more legal citations per document (right).
The citation verification burden affects not just filers.
Attorneys already cite the lack of time as a reason for not carefully checking AI-generated citations in their own filings.

kp.k: Citation checking requires five distinct error checks
kp.d: The study develops a taxonomy grounded in court filings: nonexistent citations, case-name mismatches, incorrect pincites, verbatim misquotes and content misrepresentation. It distinguishes meaning-preserving quotation changes from substantively unsupported propositions. Although these errors can coexist in practice, dataset construction introduces only one error type per citation. The task therefore extends beyond confirming case existence or checking Bluebook formatting to checking quotation accuracy, page support and legal propositions.
qs: Non-existent citation. The citation does not correspond to any real case.
Case name mismatch. The reporter citation and case name refer to two different real cases.
Verbatim misquote. The exact quoted language does not appear in the cited case.
Content misrepresentation. A cited case exists but does not support the proposition for which it is cited.

kp.d: The dataset contains 1,300 entries: 1,000 excerpts from 245 federal appellate briefs filed in 13 U.S. Courts of Appeals during January 2012–December 2021, plus 300 manually checked holdings entries from Dahl et al. (2024). It includes 4,499 citation instances, of which 1,107 contain hallucinations. Errors occur in 500 of the appellate excerpts, deliberately creating a balanced evaluation subset rather than reproducing real-world prevalence. All evaluations use a 390-example test set following a 70–30 split. The task measures extraction of erroneous spans with relaxed substring matching, not the quality of legal advice generally.
qs: Across the full dataset, there are 4,499 total citation instances, of which 1,107 citation instances contain hallucination.
We choose this ratio to create a balanced evaluation set, which does not reflect the real hallucination rate observed in generated legal documents.
We run all evaluations on the test set, which contains 390 examples.

kp.k: Agentic retrieval improves recall, not uniformly overall performance
kp.d: The authors evaluate five models in a BOED agent framework with legal-database and web tools, natural-language belief tracking and a 30-step limit, alongside non-agentic baselines. GPT-5 achieves 84.4% recall, 40.8% precision and 55.0% F1, compared with 58.2%, 36.9% and 45.2% without the harness—a 26.2-percentage-point recall increase. All five models improve recall, but Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen3-8B have lower agentic F1 scores. A separate Claude Code/Opus 4.8 comparison achieves the highest precision and F1, at 76.1% and 68.8%, with 62.8% recall; it uses its own harness and permits multiple tool calls per turn.
qs: The BOED agentic harness achieves higher recall than non-agentic experiments.
Claude Code agent achieves the highest precision and as a result, the highest F1 score, while its recall is lower than GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B’s.

kp.k: Pincites remain particularly difficult to check
kp.d: Table A6 reports GPT-5 recall of 100.0% for nonexistent citations and case-name mismatches, 52.8% for incorrect pincites, 95.2% for verbatim misquotes and 83.2% for content misrepresentation. Claude Code's incorrect-pincite recall is 3.6%. The results discussion identifies wrong pincites as a persistent weakness and links it to unavailable pagination; 19.9% of retrieved opinions contain no usable text or lack pagination. The conclusion instead calls content misrepresentation the hardest category across systems, so the source's general characterization is not fully consistent with its reported category results.
qs: Page number information for many cases is only accessible through Westlaw and LexisNexis, which explains why models perform the worst on this category.
Out of all the opinions retrieved by all agents, 19.9% of them contain no usable text or lack pagination information.

kp.k: Database gaps cause false hallucination accusations
kp.d: The authors attribute substantial checking limitations to incomplete public case repositories, proprietary identifiers and missing official pagination. Among 132 correct distinct test citations unavailable through CourtListener lookup, Gemini 2.5 Flash falsely flags 65.9% and GPT-5 25.0%. Stronger agents seek alternative evidence or preserve uncertainty instead of equating a failed lookup with fabrication. Claude Code sometimes locates opinion content without validating the citation identifiers themselves. The authors recommend broader public access or systems built on commercial databases; their experiments do not quantify the gains from either intervention.
qs: The test set contains 132 correct distinct citations that return no lookup result on CourtListener.
Additionally, public repositories sometimes lack official re- porter pagination, which originates in commercial publisher formatting.
However, this approach comes with the caveat that the citation identifiers themselves are not verified, only the content of the case is.

kp.k: Agent costs and reliability constrain practical deployment
kp.d: GPT-5 averages 15.3 steps per excerpt and reaches the 30-step limit in 29.5% of test episodes. In the authors' selected-category error analysis, exhausted budgets account for 36.7% of false negatives and reliability failures for 30.6%. Duplicate citation lookups and opinion searches occur in 39.7% and 26.4% of episodes respectively. Reliability failures include malformed output, premature termination and missed citation-related content. Claude Code averages 15.4 tool calls per excerpt, with 7.4% exact duplicates, but 21.5% of CourtListener calls are invalid. These findings concern short excerpts rather than successful full-brief deployment.
qs: GPT-5 hit the step limit on 29.5% of test episodes, which suggests that a higher step budget could further improve recall.
These redundant searches consume budget without making actual progress.
However, 21.5% of its CourtListener tool calls are invalid.

kp.k: Pro se support requires more than sanctions
kp.d: The authors argue that unrepresented litigants face disproportionate risks because they may lack both awareness of fabricated citations and access to commercial research resources. They report courts responding with sanctions, dismissals and AI-disclosure requirements, but recommend targeted AI literacy, practical citation-checking guidance, freely accessible case law and automated checking assistance. They contrast U.S. fragmentation with CanLII's generally complete Canadian coverage for cases decided after 2001. Their warning that unsupported pro se litigants may abandon AI, or find professional representation cheaper and less risky, is a conditional prediction rather than an observed outcome.
qs: Courts already provide resources for pro se litigants.
Second, expanding public, freely-available access to legal data (including all case law) would improve both human and automated citation veri- fication performance for under-resourced filers.
Facing significant sanctions for potential AI hallucinations and no reliable way to verify citations, pro se litigants may eventually abandon AI altogether.

kp.k: Checking tools could support courts and procurement
kp.d: The authors propose agentic citation checking as assistance for draft review and court screening, not as demonstrated autonomous legal judgment. The agents surfaced over 10 human-made citation errors in pre-LLM briefs, suggesting usefulness beyond AI-generated documents. The authors also propose using the benchmark to audit tools for public-agency procurement and suggest law clerks may assume expanded checking responsibilities as AI-generated filings grow. These applications remain proposals subject to reliability, data-access and long-document limitations.
qs: The agent surfaced over 10 citation typos in pre-LLM briefs that human authors missed.
Our findings suggest that agentic systems can support this work by flagging errors in draft briefs before filing or assisting law clerks in screening submitted documents.
It can further be used to audit existing citation verification tools to inform procurement processes of public agencies.

kp.k: Benchmark results require substantial generalization qualifications
kp.d: The authors explicitly caution that semi-synthetic errors and short excerpts may not represent naturally occurring hallucinations in full filings. They describe the benchmark as a controlled lower bound on difficulty and encourage testing natural examples and longer documents; their longest collected brief has 193 pages, more than 30,000 words and over 1,000 citations. They also revise ground-truth labels after reviewing GPT-5 false positives and add optional labels for ambiguous errors: matching predictions receive credit, while omissions incur no false-negative penalty. These choices qualify interpretation of the reported scores.
qs: Our benchmark should primarily be treated as a controlled lower bound on verification difficulty.
The longest brief we collected contains 193 pages, more than 30,000 words, and over 1,000 citations.
An optional ground truth segment means that a prediction matching these spans counts as a true positive, but failing to predict them does not count as a false negative.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Liu, Stammbach and Henderson argue that AI-generated legal drafting creates a persistent and growing citation-checking burden, while agentic citation-checking systems offer useful but incomplete assistance.
pts.d: The authors claim that legal citation hallucinations are not consistently declining across model generations and that identified court filings containing fabricated citations continue to grow despite sanctions. They argue that newer models produce more citations and draw on less canonical cases, increasing the work needed to check legal documents. Invoking a Jevons-paradox mechanism, they predict that cheaper drafting is likely to increase filing volume, potentially increasing total checking work even if individual hallucination rates improve. Their benchmark shows that agentic retrieval increases detection recall relative to non-agentic baselines, but performance varies across models and error categories. GPT-5 has the highest recall, whereas Claude Code with Opus 4.8 has the highest precision and F1. The authors further argue that incomplete public legal databases and missing pagination constrain automated checking. They propose improved public access, targeted AI literacy for unrepresented litigants, and automated checking tools as structural responses. They suggest that agents can assist rather than replace people checking draft briefs or screening filed documents, and that law clerks may acquire an expanded role.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their claims with a controlled drafting experiment, a compilation of court incidents, a semi-synthetic detection benchmark, and agent error analysis; broader market and policy consequences are arguments or predictions.
pts.d: The drafting experiment uses eight ChatGPT model generations, 92 prompts derived from filings flagged for hallucinations, and more than 8,000 generated case citations checked against CourtListener and Westlaw. The authors report approximately 25% hallucinated citations for earlier GPT-3.5 models, a low of 1.23% for mid-2024 GPT-4o, and 6.57% for GPT-5.1, with p = 0.001 for comparison with the August 2024 GPT-4o release. These generation rates concern nonexistent cases and case-name/reporter mismatches, not all forms of legal inaccuracy. Separately, their research combined with public datasets identifies over 1,000 filings containing hallucinated citations; this incident compilation is distinct from measured model error rates. LePhantomCite contains 1,300 entries: 1,000 appellate-brief excerpts with systematically injected errors and 300 manually checked holdings drawn from Dahl et al. The test set contains 390 examples. GPT-5 with BOED achieves 84.4% recall, 40.8% precision and 55.0% F1, versus non-agentic recall of 58.2%—a 26.2 percentage-point increase. Claude Code with Opus 4.8 achieves 62.8% recall, 76.1% precision and 68.8% F1. GPT-5's category recalls are 100% for nonexistent citations and case-name mismatches, 52.8% for incorrect pincites, 95.2% for verbatim misquotes and 83.2% for content misrepresentation. Agents retrieved opinions lacking usable text or pagination in 19.9% of instances. GPT-5 averages 15.3 steps per excerpt and reaches the 30-step limit in 29.5% of episodes. The authors also report finding over 10 human-made citation typos in pre-LLM briefs. Court decisions provide qualitative evidence of burdens, sanctions and litigants' difficulties. The proposed effects of open data, education, expanded clerk roles and potential abandonment of AI are not established by intervention trials or labour-market measurements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The measured findings concern specified model releases and short-excerpt experiments; the wider consequences are conditional predictions without a fixed deadline.
pts.d: The supplied 2026 paper examines ChatGPT releases spanning late 2023 through late 2025. Its source appellate briefs date from January 2012 through December 2021 to minimise AI contamination. The drafting experiment's hallucination definition excludes unsupported propositions attached to real cases, so the authors describe it as a conservative measure. Detection experiments use short excerpts, a 70–30 train/test split, and a 30-step BOED budget; Claude Code instead has 30 turns and can make multiple tool calls per turn. The authors explicitly state that the constructed error prevalence does not represent real-world prevalence and that semi-synthetic results may not generalise fully to actual filings. They frame the benchmark as a controlled lower bound on checking difficulty, with reliability and resource problems expected to worsen on long, citation-dense briefs. The predicted increase in filing volume depends on cheaper drafting stimulating use. Benefits from automated checking depend on sufficient access to legal data and improved reliability. Potential abandonment of AI by pro se litigants depends on continued escalation of sanctions without remedies for structural barriers. No fixed dates are given for these prospective changes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify burdens on litigants, attorneys, opposing counsel and courts, with disproportionate disadvantages for unrepresented and under-resourced filers.
pts.d: Attorneys, judges and pro se litigants use AI to draft legal documents. When filers fail to check citations, opposing counsel, law clerks and judges must absorb that work. Courts face wasted resources and potentially distorted legal arguments. Law clerks may take on more screening work, supported by agents that flag possible errors. Pro se litigants can benefit from improved ability to draft pleadings and pursue legal claims, but the authors describe them as particularly exposed to fabricated authorities because of limited awareness, legal expertise and access to subscription databases. They predict that sanctions coupled with inadequate checking resources may cause such litigants to abandon AI, or make professional representation comparatively cheaper and less risky. Professional parties with research subscriptions and established checking practices are better positioned to use AI responsibly. Developers of citation-checking systems inherit public-data coverage gaps, and public agencies could use the benchmark to audit tools during procurement. These are claims about litigation work and access to justice, not quantified predictions about law-firm staffing or revenues.
